evaluation_dimensions.name: Architecture
evaluation_dimensions.description: Technical stack, model‑guardrails, isolation mechanisms, and integration points for prompt‑injection mitigation (e.g., sandboxing, token‑level filtering). Includes on‑prem vs. cloud native designs. [doc_001]

evaluation_dimensions.name: Enterprise Latency / Throughput
evaluation_dimensions.description: Measured end‑to‑end response time and sustained request per second (RPS) under typical healthcare workloads (EHR query bursts, imaging metadata). Captures any latency added by defense layers. [doc_002]

evaluation_dimensions.name: Pricing Predictability
evaluation_dimensions.description: Structure of fees (per‑token, per‑call, subscription), volume discounts, and any hidden costs for false‑positive handling or additional logging. Important for budget‑constrained health systems. [doc_003]

evaluation_dimensions.name: Advertised vs. Actual SLA
evaluation_dimensions.description: Comparison of vendor‑published service‑level agreements (uptime, latency caps, false‑positive rate guarantees) against independently verified performance data or third‑party audit reports. [doc_004]

evaluation_dimensions.name: On-Prem / Hybrid Readiness
evaluation_dimensions.description: Degree of support for deployment behind firewalls, edge devices, or hybrid cloud orchestrations required by HIPAA‑compliant facilities. Includes containerization, air‑gap options, and data residency controls. [doc_005]

evaluation_dimensions.name: Customer Sentiment & Trust
evaluation_dimensions.description: Qualitative and quantitative signals from healthcare clients (NPS, case studies, security incident histories) that reflect confidence in the defense’s efficacy and false‑positive handling. [doc_006]

sources.purpose: Obtain architecture diagrams, claimed throughput numbers, pricing tables, and SLA language.

sources.type: Third‑Party Benchmark Reports (e.g., Gartner, Forrester, IDC)
sources.purpose: Validate advertised performance and capture independent false‑positive rate measurements.
Confirm on‑prem/hybrid readiness and data residency claims.
Gather sentiment, trust indicators, and real‑world false‑positive experiences from healthcare organizations.
Identify undocumented edge cases, community‑reported bugs, and peer‑reviewed mitigation effectiveness.

actions: Download the latest whitepapers from each vendor website.
Request pricing guides and SLA contracts via sales outreach.
Acquire relevant analyst reports through corporate subscriptions.
Deploy each solution in a controlled testbed replicating typical healthcare API traffic.
Run standardized prompt‑injection attack vectors (e.g., jailbreak prompts, token injection) at varying loads.
Record latency, throughput, and false‑positive counts.
Conduct semi‑structured interviews with 5–7 CIO/CTO or security leads from hospitals using each product.
Distribute a Likert‑scale survey covering trust, support responsiveness, and perceived false‑positive impact.
Map vendor‑claimed metrics to benchmark results; flag discrepancies >10 %.
Compare SLA terms to observed uptime logs from public status pages or third‑party monitoring services.
Score each dimension on a 0‑5 scale using a weighted rubric (e.g., latency 20 %, pricing 15 %).
Produce a comparative matrix and executive summary highlighting Veloce Security’s relative strengths/weaknesses in healthcare settings.

competitor_profiles.name: CloudScale AI
competitor_profiles.positioning: Provides an enterprise‑grade agent orchestration plane with a Gateway that handles semantic caching, token optimization, and intelligent load balancing across 14 LLM backends, targeting mid‑to‑large engineering enterprises migrating multi‑agent systems to production.

competitor_profiles.name: DataPulse Systems
competitor_profiles.positioning: Builds real‑time streaming data infrastructure and feature stores that connect Apache Kafka, Flink, and vector databases directly to agentic execution engines, serving financial institutions, fraud‑detection teams, and high‑frequency real‑time analytics workloads.

competitor_profiles.name: NexusOps Technologies
competitor_profiles.positioning: Offers an autonomous AIOps platform that automates IT incident triage, telemetry correlation, and self‑healing runbook remediation via multi‑agent graphs, aimed at DevOps, SRE, and platform‑engineering organizations managing Kubernetes at scale.

competitor_profiles.name: Veloce Security
competitor_profiles.positioning: Develops the leading AI runtime firewall for agentic applications, providing sub‑15 ms prompt‑injection defense, jailbreak mitigation, and PII sanitization, focused on healthcare, legal, and other compliance‑sensitive enterprises.

quotes.quote: CloudScale reduced our Groq and OpenAI token costs by 28% within the first month. However, documentation for custom Python middleware is sparse, and we experienced two 3-hour outages in Q2 where support disputed our 10x SLA credit claim citing upstream cloud network degradations.

The semantic cache hit rate hovers around 22% in production, which is lower than the advertised 40%. The UI dashboard is intuitive, but on-prem installation took four weeks instead of the promised 48 hours.

DataPulse is unrivaled for real-time latency. Our fleet routing agents query fresh sensor states in 6ms. Be careful with high-volume Kafka topics, however; overage fees doubled our invoice in month three before we configured filtering.
Reduced our MTTR from 45 minutes to 11 minutes for recurring database and pod connection incidents. The safety guardrails are solid—it has never accidentally executed an unsafe command in production.

Veloce caught three sophisticated indirect prompt injection attempts during our clinical pilot. The false positive rate on medical abbreviations is slightly annoying (around 4%), but their customer support helped tune custom bypass dictionaries quickly.

outages_and_incidents.description: Two separate three‑hour service outages occurred in Q2; the customer’s request for a 10× SLA credit was denied by support, who attributed the failures to upstream cloud network degradations.

praise_and_positive_outcomes.description: Achieved a 28 % reduction in Groq and OpenAI token costs within the first month of deployment.
Mean time to recovery (MTTR) dropped from 45 minutes to 11 minutes for recurring database and pod‑connection incidents; safety guardrails prevented any unsafe command execution in production.
Detected three sophisticated indirect prompt‑injection attempts during a clinical pilot, demonstrating strong security coverage.
Delivered sub‑10 ms latency for real‑time fleet routing queries, highlighting superior performance for latency‑sensitive workloads.
User interface dashboard described as intuitive, facilitating easier monitoring and management.

usability_and_friction_points.description: Documentation for building custom Python middleware is described as sparse, creating integration friction.
Observed semantic cache hit rate of 22 % versus the advertised 40 %; on‑premise installation required four weeks, far exceeding the promised 48‑hour timeframe.
High‑volume Kafka topics triggered unexpected overage fees that doubled the invoice in month three before proper filtering was applied.
False‑positive rate on medical abbreviations is around 4 %, which users find slightly annoying despite support assistance.
